picks.style: ancient greek tragic chorus, lyre and aulos, frame drum, layered female voices, slow processional lament, building
picks.why: The chorus's own invocation to the Muse and the wooden horse dragged singing through the gates — a self-contained ballad of the fall.

picks.style: ancient greek threnody, bowed lyre, low drone, single female voice with answering chorus, mournful, sparse
picks.why: "Gone are your sacrifices! gone the dancer's cheerful shout!" — anaphora built for singing, and the accusation flung at Zeus.

picks.style: ancient chorus ode, double flute, harp, high female voices in unison, wistful, flowing
picks.why: Ganymede pouring wine while his birthplace burns, then "Ah! Love, Love" — the most lyric image in the play.

picks.style: hellenistic art song, kithara, soft hand drum, solo female voice, sensual, unhurried
picks.why: "Who gave soul to the stone?" and Aphrodite's own outraged "Where did Praxiteles see me naked?" — the anthology's most quoted epigrams.

picks.style: greek erotic lyric, lyre and double flute, light tenor, playful, quickening
picks.why: Naked laughing Eros with earth in one hand and sea in the other, closing on "light it from my soul; for I am all aflame".

picks.style: greek symposium drinking song, barbitos lyre, tambourine, ragged warm male voice, tipsy, swaying
picks.why: Anacreon staggering with one slipper lost — the refrain "Guard the old man, Bacchus, lest he fall" is already a chorus.

picks.style: english hymn, chamber organ, viola da gamba, gentle tenor, slow, consoling
picks.why: "Come, peace of mind, delightful guest!" — a complete stanzaic ode by the author of the Olney Hymns, made to be sung.

picks.style: georgian sacred air, harpsichord and strings, grave baritone, measured, sombre
picks.why: "Ask what is human life" — six couplets that answer the question and close on darkness and despair.

picks.style: pastoral blank-verse air, acoustic guitar and low strings, plain weathered male voice, steady, turning
picks.why: The threshing floor and "By ceaseless action, all that is, subsists" — a working image that becomes a cosmology.

picks.style: georgian parlour song, harpsichord and cello, bright soprano, lilting, gently mocking
picks.why: An actual song in ballad stanzas, and its point lands clean: all can discern a face that's fair, but few a lovely mind.

picks.style: 18th century comic air, fortepiano, wry mezzo-soprano, brisk, conversational
picks.why: The poet at her mirror deciding Medusa's snakes were only grey hair — self-contained and genuinely funny.

picks.style: english pastoral folk ballad, acoustic guitar and recorder, warm female vocal, unhurried, sunlit
picks.why: The Ode to May in trochaic quatrains — shepherd, broom, wild thyme; the most singable thing in the set.

picks.style: georgian elegy, harp and muted strings, clear soprano, slow, aching
picks.why: Gilded captivity in the Happy Valley: "Variety, thou dear, but distant name!" — longing with a real image behind it.

picks.style: evening hymn, chamber organ and viol, hushed female voice, slow, spacious
picks.why: Silence, Fancy crossing the trackless realms of space, and the hail to Solitude — a devotional stanza set that stands alone.

picks.style: 18th century hymn tune, chamber organ, viola, sweet tenor, gentle, flowing
picks.why: Clean common-metre stanzas on the beam that "can make the bed of sickness please, and stop the sense of pain".

picks.style: penitential hymn, low organ and cello, dark baritone, slow, severe
picks.why: The Barreaux sonnet's terrible logic — "Thy majesty prevents my bliss, thy grace demands my doom" — and the sinner inviting the bolt.

picks.style: greek romance idyll, kithara and soft flute, warm tenor, flowing, ornamented
picks.why: Only candidate, but its first half is a genuine set piece: the rose as king of the flowers, blush of the meadow.

picks.style: german student lied, upright piano, light male voice with small chorus, brisk, wry
picks.why: Only candidate, and it happens to be a rhymed epigram-quatrain on the Homeric question — short, closed, singable.
